sources.note: Not re-read for this round: the MSCS course's dated unit source (REQ-245, read 2026-11-11) records 'deadlock needs all four conditions at once: mutual exclusion, hold-and-wait, no preemption, circular wait; preventing any one prevents deadlock'. The case's fix, acquiring locks in one global order, prevents circular wait; a lock with a timeout and back-off gives up hold-and-wait at a cost in retries.

Harbor Mutual Bank (fictional), its service, queue sizes, timings and cutoff are invented teaching values. Thread dumps and test output are authored renderings in each tool's style; the facts they carry are the source's.

brief.situation: You are the on-call engineer for ledgerd at Harbor Mutual Bank (fictional), the Python service whose 8 worker threads move money between accounts. Each transfer locks the source account, then the destination, then writes both balances. Since 16:35 no transfer has completed and the queue is growing. Transfers not completed by the 17:30 same-day cutoff roll to tomorrow. It is 16:40.
handover: Customers often send money back and forth between their own accounts at month-end.
The database reports no lock waits of its own: the locks are the service's in-memory account locks.
howItWorks: Pick a command or a change from the action list. Nothing you pick is typed or executed: every step shows an authored result.
Each step takes working minutes, and the clock moves by the minutes it takes. The cutoff runs on the same clock.
The screen shows the alert lines, the services and the link between them, and the result of each step.
When you close the incident you record what you found and explain your reasoning.

writeup.question: For the incident review: why transfers stopped, which condition your fix removes, and how you know it holds.

parts.label: Why they stopped
parts.criteria: A deadlock, shown by the thread dump: worker-1 holds account 1042 and waits for 2210 while worker-2 holds 2210 and waits for 1042. All four conditions hold: mutual exclusion, hold-and-wait, no preemption, circular wait. Not load (0% CPU) and not the database.
parts.modelAnswer: Opposite transfers took the same two locks in opposite orders, so they waited on each other forever.

parts.label: Which condition the fix removes
parts.criteria: A global lock order (lower account first) makes a circular wait impossible; a timeout with back-off removes hold-and-wait at the cost of retries; one global lock removes concurrency and misses the cutoff; more threads or restarts remove nothing.
parts.modelAnswer: Lock order by account number: every thread acquires in the same order, so no cycle can form.

parts.label: How you know
parts.criteria: A concurrency test that reproduces the cycle (opposite pairs on many threads) passes on the patched code before deploying, with balances unchanged; then the queue drains.
parts.modelAnswer: 10,000 opposite pairs on 8 threads: 0 deadlocks, totals unchanged; queue drained by 17:08.

fixed.headline: Good: the cycle cannot form
fixed.body: Zero CPU and threads asleep on locks meant blocked, not busy. The dump showed two locks taken in opposite orders. A global lock order removes the circular wait, the one condition you can cheaply break, and the test proved it before it shipped.

fixedGaps.headline: Fixed, with gaps
fixedGaps.body: Transfers flow, but the fix traded something: retries from a timeout, all concurrency from a global lock, a missed cutoff, or a deploy before the cause was seen or the test passed.

stillStuck.headline: Still deadlocking
stillStuck.body: A restart clears the waiters, and the next pair of opposite transfers makes the same cycle within minutes. More threads add more chances to meet. Only removing a necessary condition stops it.

lost.headline: Customer transfers thrown away
lost.body: The blocked transfers were valid work waiting on a bug. Fix the locking and let them retry.

time_up.headline: Time up
time_up.body: Nothing was recorded before the case's limit.

scoring.modelReasoning: Eight threads asleep at 0% CPU with the queue growing means blocked, not overloaded. The thread dump shows worker-1 holding account 1042 and waiting for 2210 while worker-2 holds 2210 and waits for 1042: a deadlock, because all four conditions hold at once (mutual exclusion, hold-and-wait, no preemption, circular wait). Restarting clears it only until two opposite transfers meet again, and more threads make that sooner. Acquire both locks in a global order (lower account number first) so a circular wait cannot form; a timeout with back-off also works but trades deadlock for retries, and one global lock trades it for all concurrency. Prove it with a concurrency test of opposite pairs before deploying, and never purge the blocked transfers.
